title: Bulge fossil fragment Terzan 5 (Webb and Hubble image)
caption: The bulge fossil fragment Terzan 5, imaged by the James Webb and Hubble Space Telescopes
credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, G. Zullo (University of Bologna), F. R. Ferraro (University of Bologna). Image Processing: A. Pagan (STScI)

recognition.text: Ranked #21 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Thousands of tiny white, orange and blue points pack this frame like a shaken snow globe. They crowd into a roughly round swarm at the center and thin out toward the edges, where a few larger orange stars carry prominent diffraction spikes. This is Terzan 5, a stellar system orbiting inside the bulge of the Milky Way, the bright, crowded central region of our galaxy that is also thick with gas and dust.

Terzan 5 was long classified as a globular cluster. Astronomers already knew it held two groups of stars of very different ages. Combining Webb and Hubble data, a team found strong evidence for two more, dating from 3.8 billion and just 2.5 billion years ago, and pinned the older groups at 12.5 billion and 4.7 billion years.

That mix proved Terzan 5 is not a globular cluster at all. It belongs to a new category, the bulge fossil fragment, a self-contained system that enriches itself, building generations of stars with different ages and iron content.
scale: Terzan 5 is 22,000 light-years away, according to ESA/Webb.

understand.summary: This combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys in visible and near-infrared light (shown in blue and cyan) with Webb's NIRCam in infrared light (shown in orange and red).
understand.eye: The Webb data are infrared and invisible to the eye, which helps see through the dust that fills the galaxy's bulge.

explore: Terzan 5 lies about 22,000 light-years away in Sagittarius. Its mass, about 2 million times the Sun's, is squeezed into a system just a few tens of light-years wide, which makes it one of the most massive and densely packed cluster-like systems in the Milky Way.
alt: A dense field of thousands of white, orange and blue stars concentrated in a roughly circular swarm at the center, with larger orange stars showing diffraction spikes near the edges.
